summary: Close encounter of the third kind: lack of reliable information.
description: Following an article published in the newspaper 'The Independent' on December 20, 1987, the gendarmerie interviewed a witness who claimed to have encountered a group of six strange people on December 12, 1987, sheltering from the rain in the ruins of a house. He exchanged a few words with them. These people reported coming from another planet, and one of them drew two symbols on the ground, which he then translated for the witness. They then climbed onto wheel-less vehicles resembling sleds. The witness heard a sound like ultrasound as the vehicles departed. Two hours after his initial observation, the witness returned to the site with his daughter and found round footprints on the ground where the figures had been. During the gendarmerie's investigation, no such footprints were found, and no further witness statements were collected. This very strange but flimsy case (a single witness, the absence of any alleged footprints) presents a few details that make the Dubious testimony: the planet of origin of the extraterrestrials ("Earth") being only a simple translation into English of the word "Terre", characters speaking approximate French, inconsistency between the description of athletes at rest and the height estimated at 1m or 1.5m. In the current classification of GEIPAN, this case is classified as PAN C due to lack of reliable information.

summary: Observation of a stationary bright point then moving slowly: lack of information.
description: On December 8, 1987, a witness observed a very bright, stationary point from their kitchen that moved slowly after about five minutes. The witness's testimony contains too little information to conduct a serious analysis.

summary: Observations over two nights of the presence of a luminous phenomenon at very low altitude: mistaken for the Moon at sunset.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named MONTFORT-SUR-MEU (35) 27.11.1987, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On November 25, 1987, around 8:20 PM (T1) and on November 27 around 11:30 PM (T2, T3, T4, T5), several witnesses observed a luminous phenomenon in the direction of the West for an extended period. This bright red object is described by some witnesses as spherical or banana-shaped. The object appears stationary or moving slowly. No noise is heard. According to the police investigation, several witnesses were interviewed. No suspicious traces were found on the ground by the police in the area. No weather balloons were launched during the indicated time window from the Rennes Saint-Jacques weather station (35). No helicopter flights were conducted at night on the days in question. This case is consistent (multiple witnesses), and the descriptions of the observed UFOs are very precise (see the investigation notes). One hypothesis is being considered: astronomical observation. The length of the observation period (up to about fifteen minutes in both cases), as well as the fact that the UFO is relatively stable or moves very slowly, are initial indicators of this type of misinterpretation. The rather clear skies also support this hypothesis. However, other details provided by the observations allow us to definitively establish the explanation of the UFO as a case of mistaken identity with the Moon: - the Moon was setting precisely in the directions of observation (the Moon was at 222nd for the first observation and at 245th for the second, while both observations were made near the pylene at around 235th). - the actual movement of the Moon (westward and toward the ground) is also consistent with the descriptions. - the UFOs observed on November 25th and 27th are described as having a large apparent diameter and being quite bright, and (especially for November 27th) according to descriptions entirely typical of the Moon, in its near-First Quarter phase, at sunset. - the colors of the two UFOs are perfectly consistent with the colors displayed by the Moon at sunset. - all five witnesses affirm that what they saw was not the Moon. However, none of them mention the Moon's position relative to the UFO, nor even whether they actually saw the Moon (e.g., T2 says, "I'm certain it wasn't the Moon. There was only one object"). This is despite the fact that the Moon was indeed in the indicated direction and not hidden by clouds, because, at least on November 27th, the sky was reported as completely clear and starry by witnesses (and by the Rennes weather station). For the first observation (T1 on November 25th), the confusion with the Moon was probably facilitated by the presence of veils of clouds (or scattered clouds), which at times partially or totally covered the Moon (which is consistent with the weather data). This allows us to explain the almost round or oval shape (and not a half-moon), the disappearance and reappearance, and also the back-and-forth movements (an optical illusion caused by the variation in intensity of the visible part of the Moon depending on the coverage and/or transparency of the veil). For November 27th, T2, T3, T4, and T5 clearly describe an object shaped like a crescent, a banana, or a half-moon, with yellow or red colors... and yet they do not recognize the Moon in a sky otherwise described as cloudless. This is a surprising element; other unreported factors may have misled the witnesses, perhaps there was a minimal amount of misleading cloud cover, but the conclusion of mistaken identity with the Moon remains unavoidable given the numerous other factors. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as A: mistaken identity with the Moon at sunset.

summary: PROBABLY A STAR (A LIGHT POINT OBSERVABLE OVER A LONG PERIOD)
description: During the nights of October 4th to 18th, 1987, a witness observed a very bright point in the sky. Following an article in the regional press, numerous other witnesses to this observation came forward. It was probably the planet Jupiter, exhibiting intense and spectacular activity along with its moons at this time of year.

summary: Observation of lights located about fifteen meters away.
description: On October 1, 1987, around 2:00 a.m., a motorist and his son spotted several lights in the countryside, several meters apart. This same observation was repeated during three successive stops. The investigation revealed that these were the headlights and two 40-watt spotlights of a tanker truck specifically equipped at the rear for milk collection.

On September 29, 1987, two witnesses observed a luminous phenomenon for a few seconds. A bright point, larger in diameter than a shooting star, moved rapidly across a very clear sky. After a nearly straight trajectory, this white point disappeared. The description suggests that it was likely an atmospheric reentry.

summary: child's account of observing an orange luminous disc with a recording of a sound.
description: On the evening of September 7, 1987, the eldest of two children in a farming family, a 10-year-old boy, went to bed, listened to a cassette on his radio cassette player, and, feeling tired, turned it off and fell asleep. Around 5:00 a.m., he was awakened by a noise: the child then saw a light through the shutters. He got up, took his radio cassette player, and turned it on to record the noise while simultaneously observing a luminous orange disc with a flashing light. The recording lasted about twenty seconds, and the luminous phenomenon disappeared shortly afterward. During the GEPAN investigation, several reconstructions were carried out, but none were truly conclusive. Samples of foliage from the birch trees where the light appeared were taken. GEPAN also took possession of the original cassette for analysis. The analysis of the cassette focused on determining how the noise had been recorded before attempting to identify it. The analysis, conducted with a device identical to the one used by the child, showed unequivocally that it was an internal recording of the device and not via its microphone. The noise therefore has nothing to do with the observed light phenomenon but originates from internal reception noise, possibly shortwave, but whose identification is no longer relevant to the GEPAN investigation. It is therefore, at best, a case of mishandling, at worst, a hoax. The biochemical analysis of the birch leaves was carried out and yielded mixed results. One of the samples showed deviations from the others in certain characteristics, which could possibly be explained by thermal or light stress, even though no deterioration was apparent on the foliage. These results are not entirely conclusive, as the analyses are not completely consistent with the parameters examined. The witness, a pre-adolescent at the time of the events, later admitted that he had fabricated the event to attract his parents' attention during a difficult period in his childhood. Subsequently, caught in the chain of events, he was unable to reverse it. This case, initially classified as category D, is reclassified as category A: a perfectly explained case of observation.

summary: Observations from two municipalities by three witnesses of the silent movement of a luminous phenomenon in the night sky: lack of information.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification within an investigation report. This case, previously classified as D and named NEUVY SUR BARANGEON (18) 1987, is part of a set of cases recently re-examined (see the investigation reports). On August 18, 1987, at approximately 10:15 PM, a resident (T1) of Nancy (18) and two residents (T2 and T3) of Vouzeron (18) observed a luminous phenomenon in the north-northwest sky from their homes. T1 described "two lights" moving together silently. T2 described the UFO as a "bright white light" shaped like a "luminous cigar" and turning towards Vierzon. T3 describes the UAP as "a large, bright white glow," and after observing it closely, he seems to see "two slightly smaller, bright white glows as well as a flashing red light" located below the UAP. T3 confirms the turn and departure towards Vierzon. Although the witnesses describe the same direction in which the UAP appeared, it is not certain that they observed the same thing, as the descriptions of observed UAPs differ, especially between T1 on the one hand, and T2 and T3 on the other. The witnesses are convinced they saw a UFO. However, the observation presents many characteristics of a misidentification of a commercial airliner: the presence of several lights, high brightness, and a turn in the trajectory. The long delay between the observation and this review of the case by GEIPAN prevents any formal identification of the aircraft responsible for the observation. Nevertheless, a Reconstruction shows that flights departing from Paris towards West Africa (for example, Dakar) regularly fly over the region where the sighting took place. It should be noted that during these overflights, the planes reach their cruising altitude and begin a turn towards the South-Southwest in the Naneay region. This change of trajectory is very consistent with the turn made by the UAP described by the witnesses. Since the planes usually fly over the area, there must have been elements that made it seem unusual compared to a typical aircraft. These elements differ according to the witnesses, even between witnesses (T2 and T3) who are certain they saw the same UAP. It seems to be: - The strong white glow (T2 and T3), a single glow for T2, a double one for T1, and also (but less distinctly, without knowing whether it was in addition to a single, stronger light) for T3. - The shape A luminous cigar shape for T2, an elongated shape for T3. Nothing of the sort for T1. - The absence of noise, the strangeness of which would stem from a limited perception of distance since the shape of the UFO is distinguishable (for T2 and T3). This dominance of white glow could result from the aircraft's (or aircraft's if there were several UFOs) headlights. It could thus be aircraft with their headlights on either after takeoff (most likely) or before landing. T1 may have seen both headlights of the same aircraft. Headlights can be switched on below 4000 m or during changes in flight level. These aircraft may not be cruising aircraft and may not be airliners. The presence of headlights could explain the perception of a luminous cigar shape through reflection on the fuselage (in the case of headlights in the wings); it is also consistent with the flashing red lights. observed by T3, also used on the ground and at low altitude by many aircraft. The failure to perceive the fixed green and red navigation lights may result from the presence of searchlights whose brightness surpasses the former. This could also explain the failure to perceive the flashing white lights, but they may not have been present as they are not mandatory for all aircraft and phases of flight. The absence of noise perception is common in cases of mistaken identity involving aircraft. It should be noted here that the wind is transverse to the direction of observation and does not contribute to noise. The observation elements would suggest an unusual flight (in this area) at low or medium altitude by one or more aircraft. We have no way of validating such a hypothesis 30 years later, but it is clear that it is possible and could produce the same perception (including multifaceted ones) for the witnesses. These testimonies and collected data lack consistency. No aeronautical survey was conducted. At the time, we had no records of angular measurements of the UFO's position in the sky or its angular size. Nothing was done to understand or validate the differences between the testimonies, nor to detect possible influences between witnesses. (They spoke to each other before giving their statements). Upon re-examination, it is not possible to classify this case as unexplained, since: - on the one hand, the aircraft hypothesis could explain it under unusual conditions (though not extreme, far from it) for the location (medium or low altitude, one or two very close aircraft). - on the other hand, the level of strangeness reported cannot be considered valid; the case is too weak. Therefore, although the aircraft hypothesis is plausible, the weak consistency of the testimonies leads us to classify the case as C: lack of reliable information.

summary: Object moving rapidly above the trees. No noise.
description: On July 29, 1987, at approximately 6:45 a.m., two witnesses in a car spotted a large, bright white mass moving rapidly above the municipal forest. This mass was the color of polished metal and was approximately 20 meters long. During the few seconds of observation, no noise or odor was noticed. This mass disappeared below the horizon. No explanation has been found.

summary: Observation of a cigar-shaped object moving at high speed.
description: On July 9, 1987, at approximately 11:55 PM, a witness observed an elongated, cigar-shaped object from their window. This observation, which lasted only a few seconds, revealed that the object was copper-red in color and moved very quickly without leaving a trace. No further sightings of this phenomenon were reported.

summary: Observation of a luminous ball for 4 to 5 seconds.
description: On March 12, 1987, at approximately 6:00 AM, a witness observed a luminous sphere for four to five seconds. With a diameter roughly equivalent to that of the full moon, this sphere moved silently, leaving behind a faint, glowing trail. No further information has been gathered regarding this phenomenon.

On the night of March 8, 1987, several witnesses heard a loud explosion around 8:40 PM. Another witness saw, just before the explosion, a red, shooting star-like object. This object moved across the sky at high speed. It was the atmospheric reentry of a meteorite.

summary: Observation of a probable atmospheric reentry
description: On January 7, 1988, at approximately 12:45 a.m., several witnesses observed a luminous phenomenon in a perfectly clear sky. Orange-white in color and resembling a crescent moon, this phenomenon suddenly disappeared with a violent explosion followed by a red dot that then faded away. It is likely that this was an atmospheric reentry.
